title: Hoon Lee on Expanding His Character in East of Eden
excerpt:
Hoon Lee explains why Zoe Kazan's adaptation gives Lee more room.
Material from a standalone episode was incorporated into other installments.
body_md:
Hoon Lee has welcomed the positive reception to East of Eden, Zoe Kazan's adaptation of John Steinbeck's novel starring Florence Pugh. For the actor, the expectations surrounding such an enduring literary work made the response particularly gratifying.

One of the adaptation's most significant changes is the expanded treatment of Lee. Kazan and writer Alexander Chee developed a standalone episode for the character, although its footage was ultimately distributed across other installments. Lee knew that his role would be expanded but did not initially know the full extent of the material.

The actor regards the decision as consistent with Steinbeck's humanism and the novel's exploration of agency and choice. Giving greater attention to historically marginalized characters, he argues, can illuminate rather than undermine the original themes. He credits Kazan's detailed knowledge of the novel for grounding her interpretation.

Lee also rejects the idea that a screen adaptation can reproduce a novel exactly. Readers construct their own mental worlds and hierarchies of attention, whereas television reflects a collective set of creative decisions. He noted that Elia Kazan's 1950s film starring James Dean omitted Lee entirely and said he had never watched that version.

For the actor, revisiting classic works allows successive generations to reconsider enduring human questions. He described playing Lee as an honor and emphasized the value of Steinbeck's nuanced characterization in challenging broad assumptions about people and history. The series debuted in October 2026 and received a positive critical response.
